question: Which patient is LEAST suitable for day-case surgery?

answers.text: A 35-year-old ASA I patient scheduled for laparoscopic cholecystectomy who lives 40 minutes from the hospital

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This patient meets the typical criteria for day surgery: ASA I, suitable procedure, and reasonable distance from the hospital with an adult escort.

answers.text: A 28-year-old ASA II patient with well-controlled asthma scheduled for excision of a skin cyst under local anaesthesia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Controlled asthma (ASA II) and a minor local anaesthetic procedure are fully compatible with day-case surgery.

answers.text: A 60-year-old ASA III patient with severe COPD and poor home support who lives alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Severe systemic disease (ASA III/IV), inadequate home support, and living alone are standard contraindications to day-case surgery. This patient requires inpatient admission.

answers.text: A 42-year-old ASA I patient undergoing inguinal hernia repair who has a responsible adult to escort them home

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Inguinal hernia repair is one of the most common day-case procedures; with an adult escort and ASA I status, this patient is an ideal candidate.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review day-case selection criteria. Medical fitness (ASA I-II preferred, controlled ASA III acceptable), adequate home support, adult escort, and proximity to hospital are all required. A patient with severe systemic disease and no home support fails multiple criteria.

Correct. Day-case contraindications include: ASA III–IV, poor home support, living alone, inability to travel, and procedures requiring prolonged monitoring. The patient's home environment is as important as their medical status.
